analysis.one_liner: Ties shipping rates between the mainland and Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and Guam to international price benchmarks.
analysis.headline: Introduced on January 23, 2025 by a Hawaii Democrat and a Guam Republican, the bill was referred to a House subcommittee and has had no markup or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: Shipping between the mainland and Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and other noncontiguous areas is dominated by a small number of US-flag carriers, and rates there run well above international levels. Current law only says those rates must be "reasonable," without defining what that means. This bill would set an objective test: a rate is reasonable if it is within 10% of a comparable international ocean rate index recognized by the Federal Maritime Commission. That would give island shippers and residents a concrete standard to challenge high freight rates.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents and businesses in Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, Guam, and other noncontiguous areas, who pay some of the country's highest ocean freight rates on nearly everything shipped in. The bill gives shippers an objective benchmark to challenge rates, and lower freight costs can flow through to store prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Island residents and shippers in noncontiguous areas

how_it_helps.text: It replaces the vague legal requirement that shipping rates merely be 'reasonable' with an objective test: a rate is reasonable if it is within 10 percent of a comparable international ocean rate index recognized by the Federal Maritime Commission.

That test applies to the noncontiguous domestic ocean trade — sea shipping between the mainland and Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and other noncontiguous areas — where a small number of carriers set rates without direct competition.
Shippers and, ultimately, consumers would have a concrete benchmark to challenge rates that run far above what the same distance costs on international routes.

analysis.who_pays: The small number of Jones Act shipping carriers that dominate the mainland-island routes, which would lose the ability to charge rates well above international levels on those lanes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Jones Act carriers on island routes

drawbacks.text: The benchmark the bill relies on — an international ocean rate index — may not be truly comparable to noncontiguous domestic routes, because carriers on those routes must use US-built, US-flagged, US-crewed ships under the Jones Act and face higher operating costs than foreign competitors; pressing rates toward international levels could squeeze the US-flag fleet's ability to maintain and replace ships.

The bill's protection only kicks in if there is a comparable international rate index the Federal Maritime Commission recognizes; if no such index exists for these routes, the standard provides little practical relief.
A fixed 10-percent band is a blunt test; it could deem rates reasonable even when they are high in absolute terms, or challenge rates that reflect real domestic service differences.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and real: residents of Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and Guam pay some of the highest ocean freight rates in the country, and the bill gives them an objective standard to challenge rates that far exceed international benchmarks. The cost falls on a small number of carriers, but the honest objection is serious: those carriers operate under the Jones Act with US crews and US-built ships, so international rates may not be a fair yardstick, and pressing rates to international levels could squeeze the US-flag fleet's finances and its reinvestment in ships. The bill's workability also depends on the Federal Maritime Commission recognizing a comparable international index, which may be difficult for these routes.

outcome.mechanism: A bipartisan pair from Hawaii and Guam introduced the bill, but the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee sent it to its maritime subcommittee, where it has sat with no markup or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ed Case (D-HI) introduced the bill with Rep. James Moylan (R-GU) as an original cosponsor on January 23, 2025.
The same day, it was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation.
Since that referral, the only recorded action is the sponsor's introductory remarks in February 2025; no markup, hearing, or vote has been scheduled.
The bill would define a 'reasonable rate' in noncontiguous domestic ocean trade as one within 10 percent of a comparable international ocean rate index recognized by the Federal Maritime Commission.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Beyond the status quo, the few carriers that set rates on mainland-to-island routes are better off so far, because they keep charging current rates while the bill sits without action in subcommittee.

for.name: Rep. Ed Case
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap noncontiguous domestic shipping rates using an international rate index.

for.name: Rep. James Moylan
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation, where no markup or vote has been scheduled since.

sides.party_line_note: A Hawaii Democrat introduced the bill with a Guam Republican as original cosponsor, and its two additional cosponsors split one from each party; no votes have been held.

industries.industry: Jones Act ocean carriers serving Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and Guam (a small number of companies)
industries.note: These carriers set rates on routes where the Jones Act shields them from foreign competition, and island shippers pay some of the highest freight rates in the country. The bill ties their rates to an international benchmark, cutting into the margin that comes from that captive market.

industries.industry: Island retailers, importers, and exporters (Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, Guam)
industries.note: Businesses that move goods by sea between the mainland and noncontiguous areas would gain a benchmark to challenge rates, and lower freight costs could be passed on to consumers. Their interest runs alongside residents who pay the prices.

The bill does not touch the Jones Act itself, but if carriers' margins on noncontiguous routes shrink, their ability to order and replace US-built ships could shrink with it. Shipbuilders have a stake in the carriers keeping their current revenue.

analysis.trajectory: With two additional cosponsors and a referral to the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation with no markup scheduled, the bill is likely to sit without action through the Congress, as most subcommittee-referred bills never reach a floor vote.
